report:
## Report: Does wax coating on apples cause cancer?

**Conclusion: The claim, as stated broadly, is false/misleading.** The wax coatings themselves (carnauba, shellac, or apples' own natural wax) are not carcinogenic — they are FDA-approved and "generally recognized as safe" (GRAS). However, there is a narrower, legitimate concern about one specific additive, morpholine, used in some wax formulations, which merits nuance rather than outright dismissal.

**Evidence for safety:** Carnauba wax and shellac are affirmed by the FDA as GRAS substances for food coatings under federal regulation, and have been used safely on produce for decades (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-184/subpart-B/section-184.1978; https://nwhort.org/fruitcoatings/). The FDA's own compliance guidance confirms components used in fruit/vegetable coatings must be regulated food additives or GRAS substances (https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/cpg-sec-562550-safety-and-labeling-waxed-coated-fruits-and-vegetables). Apples also naturally produce their own wax layer, which is removed and often replaced during processing — not an inherently toxic addition (https://www.snopes.com/news/2018/09/18/breakdown-everything-wrong-shocking-secrets-food-industry-viral-video/).

**The morpholine nuance:** Some conventional wax coatings use morpholine as an emulsifier. Morpholine can theoretically convert to N-nitrosomorpholine, a nitrosamine linked to cancer in animal studies. However, McGill University's Office for Science and Society notes formation of this compound in the human stomach after eating treated apples is "highly unlikely," and IARC concluded evidence for morpholine's own carcinogenicity was inadequate (https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/critical-thinking-health-and-nutrition/waxing-lyrical-about-fruit-wax). Notably, morpholine is not authorized as a food additive in the EU, reflecting a precautionary rather than confirmed-danger stance.

**Bottom line:** Wax coatings generally are safe and regulator-approved; the cancer claim conflates a theoretical, low-probability pathway involving one specific additive (morpholine) with the broader, false generalization that "wax causes cancer." Washing produce remains reasonable practice regardless.
